title: Faulty Sensor
statement:
Two sensors record the same sequence of measurements at the same time: `sensor1[i]` and `sensor2[i]` are the `i`-th readings of sensor 1 and sensor 2. A broken sensor loses exactly one reading: every reading after the lost one moves one position to the left, and the now-empty last position holds an arbitrary value that is guaranteed to be **different from the lost reading**.

At most one of the two sensors is broken, and the input always fits this description. Return `1` or `2`, the number of the broken sensor. Return `-1` when neither sensor is broken, or when both sensors could explain the data equally well so the broken one cannot be identified.
notes:
## Intuition

Up to the first position where the sensors disagree, both copies are trustworthy. From there on, a broken sensor reads one step **ahead** of the healthy one: its value at `j` is the healthy sensor's value at `j + 1`. So test both possibilities with a pair of indices `j` and `j + 1` walking right together. If exactly one sensor fits the "one step ahead" pattern, it is the broken one; if both fit (or the arrays never really disagree before the last slot), the data cannot decide.

A brute force would try every lost position in each sensor and rebuild the array, which is O(n²).

## Approach

1. Move `i` right while the readings agree, stopping at the last index at the latest.
2. Assume both `firstFaulty` and `secondFaulty` until disproved.
3. For each `j` from `i` to `n - 2`: sensor 1 can be broken only if `sensor1[j] === sensor2[j + 1]`; sensor 2 only if `sensor2[j] === sensor1[j + 1]`.
4. If both flags agree, return `-1`; otherwise return the sensor whose flag survived.

## Example 1, step by step

`sensor1 = [2,3,4,5]`, `sensor2 = [2,1,3,4]`. They agree at index 0, so `i = 1`.
- `j = 1`: `sensor1[1] = 3` equals `sensor2[2] = 3` (sensor 1 still possible); `sensor2[1] = 1` differs from `sensor1[2] = 4`, so `secondFaulty = false`.
- `j = 2`: `sensor1[2] = 4` equals `sensor2[3] = 4`.

Only `firstFaulty` survives, so the answer is `1`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): each index is visited once by `i` or `j`.
- Space: O(1): two flags and two indices.

## Pitfalls

- A difference only in the last slot is always ambiguous: either sensor could have lost its final reading.
- Alternating data such as `[3,1,3,1,3]` vs `[1,3,1,3,1]` fits both shifts, so the answer is `-1`.
- Do not stop at the first index where one shift fits; the pattern must hold all the way to `n - 2`.
- Identical arrays mean no sensor is broken, which is also `-1`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n` | number of readings per sensor |
| `i` | first index where the sensors disagree (at most `n - 1`) |
| `j` | index walking through the shifted part; compared with `j + 1` |
| `firstFaulty` | sensor 1 still fits "lost one reading" |
| `secondFaulty` | sensor 2 still fits "lost one reading" |

narration.2: Both sensors have the same number of readings, n.
narration.4: Skip the prefix where both sensors agree; stop at the last index at the latest.
narration.5: This position matches, so it tells us nothing; move on.
narration.7: Assume sensor 1 could be the broken one until a reading disproves it...
narration.9: Walk j through the rest, always comparing position j with position j + 1 of the other sensor.
narration.10: A broken sensor 1 would be one step ahead: its j-th reading must equal sensor 2's (j+1)-th.
narration.11: The shift does not fit, so sensor 1 cannot be the broken one.
narration.13: Likewise, a broken sensor 2 must be one step ahead of sensor 1.
narration.14: The shift does not fit, so sensor 2 cannot be the broken one.
narration.17: If both sensors (or neither) fit the pattern, the data cannot single one out.
narration.18: Report that the faulty sensor cannot be determined.
narration.20: Exactly one sensor fits the shift; return its number.
